pointOfInterests.description: The Grave Creek put-in is located downstream river right of the Grave Creek confluence and just downstream of the high bridge where Galice Road crosses the river. This access represents the start of the wild classified section of the Wild and Scenic River where permits are required. This access is only open for day use and many groups utilize one of the launch points upstream that allow staging the day before and camping the night before launching.
pointOfInterests.name: Grave Creek Put-in

pointOfInterests.description: Just downstream of the Grave Creek boat ramp, the main channel flows down the left side of the river. Follow the main current down the tongue.
pointOfInterests.name: Grave Creek Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A vertical drop formed by a ledge. Follow the main tongue left of center to avoid rocks on the right.
pointOfInterests.name: Grave Creek Falls

pointOfInterests.description: A wide bedrock ledge blocks the river creating a 10-12' drop. The main current flows steeply over the left side into powerful reversals (class V). Scattered boulders guard the middle and right side of the river at the top of the rapid, but a route exists through the rocks to a center chute (class IV+). A narrow and shallow fish ladder was blasted into the bedrock on the far river right side which serves as the most common route through the rapid (class III). On busy days, raft traffic can get backed up at the fish ladder. Be sure the route is clear before committing and pay careful attention to oar management to avoid breaking one. At lower flows both the center chute and fish ladder become tight for big rafts.
pointOfInterests.name: Rainie Falls

pointOfInterests.description: Named for Chinese miners who worked in the canyon, this rapid is a straightforward read and run.
pointOfInterests.name: China Gulch Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A long and wide gravel bar on the left pushes the river against the right side. The channel curves back to the left, then splits around a large midstream boulder. Take care to avoid the ledge holes that form in this rapid.
pointOfInterests.name: Tyee Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: The river splits around a long island and picks up speed. The preferred line is generally down the right but the left line is possible. When the channels converge the river bends to the right through the main part of the rapid.
pointOfInterests.name: Wildcat Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A long, splashy rapid with multiple channels particularly as flows increase. The main current is generally straightforward down the left, but midstream rocks and shifting hydraulics reward staying alert and reading ahead.
pointOfInterests.name: Russian Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A moderate rapid with a defined tongue leading into wave trains and scattered boulders. Clean lines are usually obvious, though higher water can push hard toward river right features.
pointOfInterests.name: Montgomery Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A narrow chute formed where Howard Creek enters from river left. The current accelerates quickly, creating a fast, technical move that demands commitment once entered.
pointOfInterests.name: Howard Creek Chute

pointOfInterests.description: As the name suggests, options are limited. This short rapid funnels into a narrow line between exposed rocks, with little room for correction if you miss the entry.
pointOfInterests.name: Slim Pickins Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: A rhythmic series of shallow waves and small ledges that create a classic “washboard” effect. Fun and splashy, but low water can make the rock dodging more technical.
pointOfInterests.name: Washboard Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A distinctive feature shaped like a blade splitting the current. Boats must choose a side early, as the central obstruction creates strong deflection and turbulence.
pointOfInterests.name: Plowshare

pointOfInterests.description: A fast, constricted chute near the Windy Creek confluence. The current piles up quickly, producing powerful waves and little margin for error, especially at higher flows.
pointOfInterests.name: Windy Creek Chute

pointOfInterests.description: Upper Black Bar Falls is a steep drop into a big curling wave. It can be scouted from the right bank.
pointOfInterests.name: Upper Blackbar Falls

pointOfInterests.description: Lower Black Bar Falls, follows the upper drop after a short distance of calm water. The lower drop is more straightforward down the main tongue to the right of center.
pointOfInterests.name: Lower Blackbar Falls

pointOfInterests.description: A short, read-and-run riffle just downstream of Black Bar Lodge. Generally straightforward, but shallow rocks can be unforgiving at lower water levels.
pointOfInterests.name: Little Windy Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: The river curves to the right around a large gravel bar, then curves back to the left around a narrow gooseneck of hillside. The current pushes against the cliffs and boulders on the outside of each curve, creating waves and turbulence. Two constrictions create bigger drops.
pointOfInterests.name: Horseshoe Bend

pointOfInterests.description: A deep, swirling pool with strong eddies and irregular currents. The development of the actual hole depends on the flow.
pointOfInterests.name: Telephone Hole Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A broad, shallow riffle with multiple small channels. The current is mellow, but low water requires careful line choice to avoid scraping over exposed rocks.
pointOfInterests.name: Dulog Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A dramatic and iconic rapid marked by a large boulder right of center that features a ledge drop followed by a hole. Line selection and boat control are critical.
pointOfInterests.name: Kelsey Falls

pointOfInterests.description: A wide riffle that marks a transition in the river’s character. Generally easy boating, though shallow gravel bars can complicate navigation at lower flows.
pointOfInterests.name: Battle Bar Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: Riffle and a river bar along the property was owned in the 1920s by famous western novelist, Zane Grey.
pointOfInterests.name: Winkle Bar - Zane Grey Cabin

pointOfInterests.description: A shallow, wave-filled riffle with a couple large boulder and scattered rocks that can appear abruptly. Straightforward at most flows, but low water requires picking a clean tongue to avoid scraping.
pointOfInterests.name: Long Gulch Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: As the name implies, this rapid is defined by large, immovable boulders that break up the flow. Expect a mix of lateral moves and splashy waves, with tighter lines at lower water.
pointOfInterests.name: Big Boulder Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: The river splits around an island, creating multiple channels. The main route is typically obvious, but boaters should choose early to avoid being pushed into shallow or rockier side channels.
pointOfInterests.name: Island Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: A gentle but rocky riffle with a steady current. It offers easy read-and-run boating, though exposed rocks can surprise inattentive boaters at low flows.
pointOfInterests.name: Johns Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A pleasant, rolling riffle with small waves and a clean tongue.
pointOfInterests.name: Maggies Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A short but more technical rapid guarded by a prominent midstream rock near the top. Precise positioning is important, as the current accelerates quickly toward downstream obstacles.
pointOfInterests.name: China Bar Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: The river enters a very narrow and scenic inner canyon. Interesting and challenging hydraulics are created by the current bouncing off the walls in the narrow confines.
pointOfInterests.name: Mule Creek Canyon - Narrows

pointOfInterests.description: The crux move in Mule Creek Canyon is the Coffee Pot where the bedrock walls constrict the flow creating a series of boils and surging eddy lines.
pointOfInterests.name: Mule Creek Canyon - Coffee Pot

pointOfInterests.description: Huge boulders block the center and right side at the top of this rapid. The main current flows down the left side, straight into a "picket fence" of boulders and sieves. You can eddy out on river right and scout from a high vantage point above the rapid. The standard move is to enter left and then cut back to the center to avoid the picket fence.
pointOfInterests.name: Blossom Bar

pointOfInterests.description: The Devils Stairs comes up quick at the end of the pool below Blossom Bar. Follow the main tongue as the river bends to the right, taking care to avoid the wall on river right.
pointOfInterests.name: Devils Stairs

pointOfInterests.description: A broad riffle with uniform wave action and mild turbulence. Lines are flexible, but shallow rocks near the edges encourage staying near the main current.
pointOfInterests.name: Tichenor Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A long, playful stretch of rolling waves that builds gradually. Fun at moderate flows through the length of the riffle.
pointOfInterests.name: Solitude Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A compact rapid that requires modest maneuvering through waves and rocks. A half dozen camps upstream of this rapid on river right are pouplar for the last night on the river. Anticipate that you will be close to other groups.
pointOfInterests.name: Tacoma Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: These are the last rapids of any significant size before Foster Bar. Clay Hill Creek comes in on the right before the rapid. The main line is down the right channel. Stay to the left side of this channel on the main tongue. Below this rapid the geology changes from volcanic to sedimentary.
pointOfInterests.name: Clay Hill Rapids

pointOfInterests.description: An easy riffle with small standing waves and a defined tongue. Usually straightforward, though low water exposes rocks that narrow the best line.
pointOfInterests.name: Payton Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A mild riffle characterized by shallow water and scattered rocks. Navigation is simple, but careful reading helps avoid scraping or unexpected bumps at lower flows.
pointOfInterests.name: Burns Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: A clean, well-defined riffle marking the transition toward calmer water downstream. Generally forgiving, with smooth wave trains and clear lines through the center. The Foster Bard take-out is just around the next bend.
pointOfInterests.name: Watson Riffle

pointOfInterests.description: The take out is on river right just past the mouth of Foster Creek.  Derig on a big, wide and treeless gravel bar.
pointOfInterests.name: Foster Bar  take out

alerts.title: Moon Complex Fire River Closure
alerts.detail: Due to the Moon Complex Fire, the Wild section of the Rogue River from Grave Creek to Foster Bar was closed to all water-based recreation on September 25th. No river permits are being issued at this time. A Forest Service closure remains in effect for the fire area, including the Bear Camp shuttle road, until conditions improve.

alerts.title: Active Rock Fall at First Stop Beach Camp (0.6 mi from Grave Creek, river Left)
alerts.detail:
My group witnessed a big rock fall event Saturday morning July 1 at 0940 on the Rogue River.

We camped at Lower Sanderson and heard rock fall on river left all night long.

When loading up Saturday morning we saw huge rocks fall into First Stop Beach camp on river left and as far out as the middle of the river. Some of the boulders were very large (like small car size). I would not camp at First Beach if you're headed down there.

alerts.title: Road Access to Grave Creek
alerts.detail: The approximately 4 mile road segment between Almeda and Grave Creek is closed to vehicle traffic due to wildfire impacts and associated slope instability. BLM is currently evaluating options to address the issues with a goal of reopening the road for the 2024 season. Both Almeda and Grave Creek are accessible by vehicle but from opposite directions (i.e. you can’t drive between them). The road itself is in good condition and suitable for walking or biking. What this means for boaters running this stretch is you can’t drive through Galice and access Grave Creek; you will instead need to launch upstream from Almeda or another access point on the run above this one. You can still launch from Grave Creek but will need to use the alternate access route that comes in from the north. This will also likely result in a higher shuttle fee if using one of the commercial services.

alerts.title: Rogue River closure - Aug/Sept 2022
alerts.detail: Due to the Rum Creek Fire, the BLM has closed access to the Rogue River upstream of Grave Creek and is making day-by-day determinations as to whether groups may launch from the Grave Creek river access to run the permitted section of the lower Rogue River (the "Wilderness Run"). For lower Rogue launch status, call 541-471-6535 (open 8 am- 3 pm) or visit the Rum Creek Fire's Facebook page for launch day closure info posted by 6 am. (https://www.facebook.com/rumcreekfire2022). Info will also be posted to the BLM website by 1 pm (https://www.blm.gov/or/resources/recreation/rogue/rogue\_river.php).

On May 4th, 2020, Grants Pass Field Manager William Dean issued a letter informing river runners that 1) the permit season on the Lower Rogue River will not be opening on May 15, 2020, 2) No self-issued permits will be allowed for the Lower Rogue River, 3) Refunds for trips that have already been paid for will be issued and the permittees will be given the same start date in 2021, 4) the recreation section of the Rogue River is still available for day use, upstream of Grave Creek. While there is no timeline for resuming issuance of permits, the BLM is prepared to issue permits once it is safe to do so.

detail.permitInfo: A float permit is available year-round for the Wild section of the Rogue River. A lottery is used to allocate the control season (May 15 - October 15) launches. Pre- and post-control season launches are obtained by filling out a self-issued permit available at Smullin Visitor Center.
detail.description:
Trips on the Rogue typically last 3-4 days and you have the unique option of camping or staying at the wilderness lodges spaced along the course of the run. The river can be run year around with the peak season being May 15th to October 15th but wonderful opportunities are available for for boating in the fall, through the winter, and in the early spring. Most of the information you'll need to plan a trip can be found on the [BLM Rogue River web site](https://www.blm.gov/programs/recreation/permits-and-passes/lotteries-and-permit-systems/oregon-washington/rogue-river). They even offer a full floater's guide in pdf format.You can either take a guided trip (some outfitters are geared towards kayakers and provide raft support for those who want to enjoy the river and have someone else worry about all the logistics) or organize your own trip. If you're interested in the latter, you will need to obtain a float permit for trips between May 15 and October 15 through the lottery, but you can also often pick up day-of permits for small group since the river is regulated by number of people launching per day rather than number of groups.

Although this is one of the nation's original Wild and Scenic Rivers that retains its ancient forests, the river has a long history of human impacts. Upstream dams decimated native salmon and steelhead runs that made this river famous, but the removal of Savage Rapids Dam, Gold Hill Dam, Gold Ray Dam, and the breaching of Elk Creek Dam offer signs of hope for fisheries recovery. On the run itself, extensive blasting during the 1930s and 1940s cleared boulders and 'cleaned up' the rapids. Finally, jet boats zip up and down the lower one-third of the run. Despite these impacts, the Rogue remains one of the Pacific Northwest's most popular multi-day whitewater trips. Warm water, great pool-drop rapids, and beautiful scenery make this a true classic.

Many trips start at one of the launch points upstream on the day stretch since the start of the wild section at Grave Creek does not provide camping options. Starting at the Grave Creek Boat Ramp (river mile 68.5, elevation 630'), class III whitewater begins immediately with Grave Creek Falls. The first major rapid, Rainie Falls (class V), comes within two miles of the put-in at an obvious horizon line. If you're thinking about running the falls you'll want to get out and scout. The best vantage is on river left and this is also the best side to portage kayaks. A class III alternative is the 'fish ladder' which is an artificial channel blasted out along river right. The 'mid chute' is a class IV chute down the middle that offers another option. All three are run depending on flows and your skill level but most people opt for the fish ladder.

The river continues with more class II and III rapids, and several excellent camps, before arriving at Rogue River Ranch. This is a good place to stop and prepare for Mule Creek Canyon at mile 21. This section offers the longest continuous whitewater on the run with good class III+ rapids through a narrow canyon that culminates in the Coffee Pot, a class IV- constriction where surging boils may require a strong brace. Soon after leaving this canyon at mile 23 you'll arrive at Blossom Bar (class IV) which is the most significant rapid on this run. You can scout the drop from the high vantage point on river right but it is hard to see all the details of the entry. During the summer season jet boats can travel upstream as far as Blossom Bar, so you are likely encounter them on the remaining 12 miles of the run.

Most boaters take out at the Foster Bar Boat Ramp (river mile 33.7) which is 34 miles from the Grave Creek put-in. The river continues 33.7 miles to the Pacific Ocean at Gold Beach, but there are fewer rapids and a road along the river.

PERMITS: Applications for the annual permit lottery (for launch dates between May 15th and October 15th) are accepted between December 1st and January 31st. You can also pick up unconfirmed launch dates by phone. Most become available ten days in advance of a launch date. Weekend launches in summer can be tough to get, but if you're flexible you can usually get a permit for a small group. Off-season permits are available by request. Additional information on permits can be found on the [Rogue National Wild and Scenic (NWS) River web site](http://www.blm.gov/or/resources/recreation/rogue/index.php).

ACCESS: The Grave Creek put-in is reached off I-5 exit 61 by heading west towards Galice. Overnight parking and camping are not allowed at the launch site. Camping and an alternative launch site can be found four miles upstream at Almeda Bar (campsite reservations for Almeda Bar are possible through [Josephine County Parks](https://www.josephinecounty.gov/parks/reservations/camping_reservations.php)). The preferred shuttle route is the Bear Camp Road (FR 23) to Foster Bar Landing. The 44-mile drive takes about two hours (one way). This option may be closed due to snow or debris slides. The long route is 193 miles and takes about five hours (one way) on Oregon Highway 199, but this is along paved roads and is open through the winter. The [BLM Rogue River web site](https://www.blm.gov/programs/recreation/permits-and-passes/lotteries-and-permit-systems/oregon-washington/rogue-river) has shuttle maps and current conditions. Many take advantage of one of the [local shuttle services](http://www.blm.gov/or/resources/recreation/rogue/shuttle-rentals.php) or a Rogue River rafting outfitter.

BEARS: Bears have become habituated to the presence of boaters in camps along the river, and there have been increasing problems with bears raiding camps for food. Please help avoid problems with bears by maintaining a clean camp, keeping food and trash secured in sealed containers, and by storing these containers within the electric bear fences at the camps where they are provided. It is not safe to store food on rafts: bears have learned to climb onto rafts in search of food. Bear fences are located at the following sites (2022 season): Whisky Creek, Horseshoe Bend, Rogue River Ranch, Upper, Middle, and Lower Half Moon Bar, Brushy Bar, Upper and Lower Solitude, Upper and Lower Tate Creek, Upper, Middle, and Lower Tacoma.
